summary: Defines a user-oriented string representation of distinguished names, the primary keys of directory entries, for use outside the directory protocol such as in mail. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 2253 and RFC 3494.

eli5.summary: A way to write an entry's full directory address as readable text.

subtitle: A readable text format for writing directory entry names.

tldr.problem: Distinguished Names in X.500 directories are encoded in ASN.1, making them unreadable when used in email or on business cards. There is no standard way to show someone the name of a directory entry as text.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a string notation using attribute type keywords (CN, O, C) separated by commas to write out the full hierarchical path to a directory entry, with optional quoting for special characters.
tldr.outcome: Directory administrators and users can now refer to entries using readable strings like 'CN=Steve Kille,O=ISODE Consortium,C=GB' instead of raw ASN.1 encoding. Later superseded by RFC 2253 which generalized the approach.

facts.label: Standard attribute keys
facts.value: CN, L, ST, O, OU, C, STREET (7 required, others can be registered)

today: RFC 1779 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 2253 and RFC 3494, which refined and generalized the syntax for broader use in LDAP and other applications.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
Distinguished Names (DNs) are the primary keys in X.500 directories, used to uniquely identify directory entries. These names are normally encoded in ASN.1 for use in directory protocols, but when a distinguished name needs to be displayed in email, on a business card, or in documentation, there is no standard human-readable format.

This RFC provides a user-oriented string representation of distinguished names that is intuitive for common cases (like people in organizations) while remaining fully general enough to represent any directory name. It aims to give a clean, readable representation that administrators and users can understand at a glance.
sections.eli5: Directory entries are like records in a filing system that need unique addresses. This notation turns those addresses into names people can read and remember.

sections.title: String Syntax
sections.content:
In this notation, a distinguished name is written as a sequence of attribute key-value pairs separated by commas. Common keys include CN (Common Name), O (Organization), C (Country), L (Locality), ST (State), OU (Organizational Unit), and STREET (Street Address). For example: CN=Steve Kille,O=ISODE Consortium,C=GB

Values with special characters (commas, equals signs, quotes) are enclosed in double quotes or escaped with backslashes. A multi-valued component—where multiple attributes together identify an entry—uses a plus sign: OU=Sales + CN=J. Smith,O=Widget Inc,C=US. For pathological cases where standard keywords do not apply, the notation supports OID (object identifier) notation and hexadecimal encoding of raw bytes.
sections.eli5: Write key=value pairs separated by commas, put quotes around values with commas in them, and use a plus sign when you need multiple things to identify the same person.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The notation was designed with five key goals in mind: provide an unambiguous representation of any distinguished name; be intuitive for the majority of names; be fully general and capable of representing any DN; support attractive layouts and formatting; and give a clear representation of what is in the name.

Unlike other syntaxes (such as the OSF Syntax used in some systems), this notation was optimized for human users rather than system configuration. It follows a hierarchical structure from most-specific to least-specific attribute (bottom-up), which matches how people think about addresses: a person's name first, then their organization, then their country.
sections.eli5: The design balances making common names easy to read with the ability to write any possible directory address correctly.

sections.title: Adoption and Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 1779 provides a practical solution for representing directory names in human-readable form. The notation became widely used in LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) and other directory applications. This representation made directory services more accessible to administrators and developers by allowing them to work with readable name strings instead of binary encodings.

The RFC is Historic and has been superseded by RFC 2253 and RFC 3494, which refined and extended the syntax to handle additional cases and better align with LDAP usage patterns.
sections.eli5: This format became so useful that it continues in modern directory systems, even though it has been improved over time.
